e-497.knowledge_point: Integrating a Logarithmic Expression Using Cyclic Integration by Parts
e-497.worked_solution:
First, we let

$$
I = \int \dfrac{\ln^2 x}{x} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{2}⁡x)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{3}⁡x-2\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{3}⁡x-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{3}⁡x-2I \\ 3I & ={ln}^{3}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

e-498.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
e-498.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J = \int e^{x}\cos{x}\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula once more, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+J \\ I & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-I \\ 2I & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

e-7313.knowledge_point: Finding the Definite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
e-7313.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I = \displaystyle \int e^{x}\sin(2x)\, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J = \int e^{x}\cos(2x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula once more, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I\mathbin.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-2{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}{5}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))}{5}-\frac{{e}^{0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0))}{5} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{\pi /2}}{5}+\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}({e}^{\pi /2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{8x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{8x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{8x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{8x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{2}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{8})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{8})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{8}-2\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{8x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{8}-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{8}-2I \\ 3I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{8} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{8x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{24}({ln}^{3}⁡x)\,{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}({ln}^{3}⁡({e}^{3})-{ln}^{3}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{24}((3\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{24}({3}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{5}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{5{ln}^{4}⁡x}{x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{5}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})(\frac{5{ln}^{4}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{4}-5\int \frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{4}-5I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{4}-5I \\ 6I & =\frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{24}({ln}^{6}⁡x)\,{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}({ln}^{6}⁡({e}^{3})-{ln}^{6}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{24}((3\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{6}-{0}^{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{24}({3}^{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{243}{8}\end{aligned}

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{9}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{9{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{9}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})(\frac{9{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9I \\ 10I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{40}({ln}^{10}⁡x){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{40}({ln}^{10}⁡(e)-{ln}^{10}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{6}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{6{ln}^{5}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{6}⁡x)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(\frac{6{ln}^{5}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{7}⁡x-6\int \frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{7}⁡x-6I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{7}⁡x-6I \\ 7I & ={ln}^{7}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{7}⁡x}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{7}({ln}^{7}⁡x){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{7}({ln}^{7}⁡(e)-{ln}^{7}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Logarithmic Expression Using Cyclic Integration by Parts
content.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{6}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{6{ln}^{5}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{6}⁡x)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(\frac{6{ln}^{5}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{7}⁡x-6\int \frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{7}⁡x-6I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{7}⁡x-6I \\ 7I & ={ln}^{7}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{7}⁡x}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{7}({ln}^{7}⁡x){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{7}({ln}^{7}⁡(e)-{ln}^{7}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

Calculate ∫ln2⁡x4xdx using integration by parts.

a
 ln3⁡x4+C
b
 −ln⁡x3+C
c
 ln⁡x12+C
d
 ln3⁡x6+C
e
 ln3⁡x12+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Set u=(ln(x))^2 and dv=dx/(4x). Then v=ln(x)/4, and integration by parts gives I=(ln(x))^3/4-2I. Solving yields I=(ln(x))^3/12+C, option e.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, we let

$$
I=\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡x(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2I \\ 3I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{12}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Calculate ∫ln2⁡x4xdx using integration by parts.

a
 ln3⁡x4+C
b
 −ln⁡x3+C
c
 ln⁡x12+C
d
 ln3⁡x6+C
e
 ln3⁡x12+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we let I=∫ln2⁡x4xdx.

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that u=ln2⁡x⇒dudx=2ln⁡xx,dvdx=14x⇒v=∫14xdx=ln⁡x4.

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

I=∫ln2⁡x4xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=ln2⁡x(ln⁡x4)−∫(ln⁡x4)(2ln⁡xx)dx=ln3⁡x4−2∫ln2⁡x4xdx=ln3⁡x4−2I.

Finally, we solve for I, remembering to add a constant of integration C at the very end: I=ln3⁡x4−2I3I=ln3⁡x4I=ln3⁡x12+C

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Logarithmic Expression Using Cyclic Integration by Parts
content.worked_solution:
First, we let

$$
I=\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡x(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2I \\ 3I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{12}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Calculate ∫e2xcos⁡xdx.

a
 e2x5(sin⁡x−2cos⁡x)+C
b
e2x5(sin⁡x+2cos⁡x)+C
c
 2e2x5(sin⁡x+cos⁡x)+C
d
 e2x5(cos⁡x−2sin⁡x)+C
e
e2x5(sin⁡x−cos⁡x)+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let I=∫e^(2x)cos(x) dx and J=∫e^(2x)sin(x) dx. Integration by parts gives I=e^(2x)sin(x)-2J and J=-e^(2x)cos(x)+2I. Substitution yields 5I=e^(2x)(sin(x)+2cos(x)), so option b is correct.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2(-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I) \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that u=e2x⇒dudx=2e2x,dvdx=cos⁡x⇒v=∫cos⁡xdx=sin⁡x.

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get I=∫e2xcos⁡xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=e2xsin⁡x−∫(sin⁡x)(2e2x)dx=e2xsin⁡x−2∫e2xsin⁡xdx=e2xsin⁡x−2J.

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate J=∫e2xsin⁡xdx.

To do this, let's suppose that u=e2x⇒dudx=2e2x,dvdx=sin⁡x⇒v=∫sin⁡xdx=−cos⁡x.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get J=∫e2xsin⁡xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=e2x(−cos⁡x)−∫(−cos⁡x)(2e2x)dx=−e2xcos⁡x+2∫e2xcos⁡xdx=−e2xcos⁡x+2I.

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for I, we can subsequently solve for I. We remember to add a constant of integration C at the end.

I=e2xsin⁡x−2JI=e2xsin⁡x−2(−e2xcos⁡x+2I)I=e2xsin⁡x+2e2xcos⁡x−4I5I=e2xsin⁡x+2e2xcos⁡xI=e2x5(sin⁡x+2cos⁡x)+C

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b. Two integrations by parts give 5I=e^(2x)(sin(x)+2cos(x)). Differentiating e^(2x)(sin(x)+2cos(x))/5 gives e^(2x)cos(x), verifying the answer.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
content.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2(-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I) \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Calculate ∫e−2xsin⁡xdx.

a
e−2x(sin⁡x+cos⁡x)+C
b
−e−2x5(2sin⁡x+cos⁡x)+C
c
2e2x3(2sin⁡x+cos⁡x)+C
d
e−2xsin⁡x−cos⁡x+C
e
cos⁡x−xsin⁡x+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let I=∫e^(-2x)sin(x) dx and J=∫e^(-2x)cos(x) dx. Integration by parts gives I=-e^(-2x)cos(x)-2J and J=e^(-2x)sin(x)+2I. Substituting gives 5I=-e^(-2x)(2sin(x)+cos(x)), so option b is correct.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2({e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I) \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
content.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2({e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I) \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6J \\ I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6({e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6I) \\ I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-36I \\ 37I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{6x}}{37}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6I.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6J \\ I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6({e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6I) \\ I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-36I \\ 37I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{6x}}{37}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}

Question 9
?

Calculate ∫e−2xcos⁡(3x)dx.

a
e−2x3cos⁡(3x)−e−x4sin⁡(3x)13+C
b
e−2x(2cos⁡(3x)−sin⁡(3x))9+C
c
e−2x(3sin⁡(3x)−2cos⁡(3x))13+C
d
e−2x(sin⁡(3x)+2cos⁡(3x))13+C
e
e2xcos⁡(3x)−2sin⁡(3x)9+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let I=∫e^(-2x)cos(3x) dx and J=∫e^(-2x)sin(3x) dx. Integration by parts gives I=e^(-2x)sin(3x)/3+2J/3 and J=-e^(-2x)cos(3x)/3-2I/3. Substitution yields 13I=e^(-2x)(3sin(3x)-2cos(3x)), so option c is correct.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}(-\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{4}{9}I \\ \frac{13}{9}I & =\frac{3{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{13}+C\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
content.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}(-\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{4}{9}I \\ \frac{13}{9}I & =\frac{3{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{13}+C\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 10
?

Calculate ∫e−xcos⁡(3x)dx.

a
e−x3cos⁡(3x)−e−x4sin⁡(3x)5+C
b
e−x(3sin⁡(3x)−cos⁡(3x))10+C
c
e−x(sin⁡(3x)+3cos⁡(3x))10+C
d
e−x(3cos⁡(3x)−sin⁡(3x))10+C
e
e−xcos⁡(3x)−3sin⁡(3x)10+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let I=∫e^(-x)cos(3x) dx and J=∫e^(-x)sin(3x) dx. Integration by parts gives I=e^(-x)sin(3x)/3+J/3 and J=-e^(-x)cos(3x)/3-I/3. Substitution yields 10I=e^(-x)(3sin(3x)-cos(3x)), so option b is correct.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}(-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{1}{9}I \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =\frac{3{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}+C\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
content.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}(-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{1}{9}I \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =\frac{3{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{10}($
{{field-1}} $)$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by  $I=\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-4x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{-4x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-4x})\,(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-\int (-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))(-4{e}^{-4x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-4x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{-4x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-4x})\,(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))-\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))(-4{e}^{-4x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2I) \\ I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-4I \\ 5I & =-{e}^{-4x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-4x}}{10}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(-\frac{{e}^{-4x}}{10}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(-\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{10}(0+1))-(-\frac{1}{10}(0+1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}-\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(1-{e}^{-4\pi }).\end{aligned}
$$
